docs.title: Introduction to OpenRefine for the Humanities and Social Sciences
docs.text:
This session will introduce participants to OpenRefine, a powerful, free and open source tool to work with large datasets. We will cover how to use OpenRefine to effectively clean and format tabular data (text and numerical data) while automatically creating a log tracking our changes. OpenRefine does all this while helping you get to know your data in depth.

This session is suitable for beginners with no prior knowledge of OpenRefine. There are no prerequisite coding skills. While the examples and data used will be aimed at the Humanities and Social Sciences community, the session is open to anyone and everyone interested in learning about OpenRefine.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
Through this short introductory lesson, you will learn:

  1. What OpenRefine is and when to use it;
  2. How to create, import and export projects in OpenRefine;
  3. How to use facets and clusters to identify typos and mistakes in your data;
  4. How to edit and transform your data; and,
  5. How to save your work and export your script.

docs.title: Download OpenRefine and the data
docs.text:
Download OpenRefine by following the instructions on their website: openrefine.org/download.

We will be using data from IMDB's collection of non-commercial datasets on movies. This data has been messed up on purpose - to give you something to fix in this lesson!

  • You can download the data here: messy_movies.csv

Instructor: Maria Sigridur Finnsdottir, PhD

This lesson is an adaptation of the Data Carpentry course "OpenRefine for Social Science Data."

docs.title: Clusters and Transformations
docs.text: In addition to the facetting, filtering, and sorting tools we've covered, you can also use OpenRefine's built-in clustering methods and transformation tools to inspect and clean your data. Clustering and transformation tools both let you change potentially large amounts of data all at once.

docs.title: Clustering
docs.text:
Clustering refers to the process of finding groups of values that could be alternative representations of the same thing; for example, “New York” and “new york”, or “Gödel” and “Godel.” Because of this, clustering is a great way to identify and clean misspelled or mistyped entries in your data.

OpenRefine has a number of built-in clustering algorithms - feel free to play around with them and see what kinds of clusters come up. Broadly speaking, they offer two categories of clustering methods: token-based (key collision, n-gram...) and character-based (Levenshtein distance, PPM...). The fingerprinting method, a key collision method, is the least likely to produce a false positive, and so is the default clustering method in OpenRefine.

You can access the clustering function by clicking the button Cluster in the top right hand corner of the facet box.

In the primary_genre text facet we created earlier, click the Cluster button. A pop-up window will appear. Towards the top of the window, you will find dropdown menus for the clustering method and keying function; for this exercise, we will start by using the default (Key collision and Fingerprint, respectively) but feel free to try different combinations and see if different clusters emerge later on.

Click on the Cluster button in the middle of the window. You should see three pairds of genre titles appear:

  • Drma <--> drma
  • Sci-Fi <-> sci-fi
  • Comedy <-> comedy

Select all the clustered pairs and press the Merge selected & re-cluster button. It should not return anymore clusters.

Note

You'll notice that you can correct the new cell value in the same step as merging; for example, you could both merge 'Drma' and 'drma' and correct their new value to 'Drama'. We are not going to do that this time, however, to get a bit more practice with clustering :)

Now, trying using different keying function and clustering method options. What other clusters appear, if any?

Solution

The combination of Key collision and Metaphone3 should return the following cluster:

  • Drama <-> Drma

Go ahead and merge these as Drama.

Close the clustering window. Now you should see that your primary_genre facet only has 23 options. Scroll through it - are there any errors that we did not catch with the clustering methods?

Solution

The various clustering functions will likely not have caught the following errors:

  • comedians
  • science fiction

These are two far away from the other genre titles, even though they refer to the same thing, and so won't be grouped in the clustering functions. These will have to be edited manually in the text facet box. Edit these entries as Comedy and Sci-Fi, respectively.

docs.title: Transforming
docs.text: Transforming data can also be a quick way to correct improperly formatted data all at once. OpenRefine includes a set of common transformations that you can use, and also allows for custom transformations. We've already encountered transformations that change data types, but there are also transformations that trim leading and trailing whitespace, or change the case of text. You can also write your own custom transformations.

docs.title: Trimming leading and trailing whitespace
docs.text:
One common use for transformations is to trim leading and trailing whitespaces. These are unnecessary, often accidental, spaces on either side of the text data in a cell. To access this transformation function, you'll need to:

  1. Open the drop down menu beside the column title;
  2. Hover over Edit cells;
  3. Hover over Common transforms;
  4. Click on Trim leading and trailing whitespace.

Try it now on the movie_title column. You should get a pop-up message confirming that you've changed 62 rows of data.

Go through the other columns of text data and make sure that there is no trailing or leading whitepace.

docs.title: Custom transformations
docs.text:
We can also write our own transformations to edit large amounts of data easily. Let's try that now to turn our sets of writer IDs and names into simple and clean lists. To do this, we'll need to remove the square brackets and quotation marks around the ID numbers and names.

Start by clicking the down arrow beside the writer_names variable title. Choose Edit cells and then Transform. This will open a pop up window for custom transformation.

You can also write your own custom transformations

This window contains a text box, where you can type a General Refine Expression Language (GREL) and use it to transform your data.

Our first step will be to remove all the square brackets. For this, type value.replace("[","") and click ok. This GREL expression is telling OpenRefine to take every "[" and replace it with "" (nothing). Helpfully, OpenRefine gives you a preview of the effect of your transformation on this

Use this same technique to remove the other square brackets (]) and the quotation marks (').

Solution

You should use the following GREL expressions:

  • value.replace("]","")
  • value.replace("'","")

After completing these two transformation, each row of writers' names should be a clean list, without any square brackets or quotation marks.

We can also string these three replacement functions together, like so value.replace(XX).replace(XX)... and so on.

Try removing the single quotation marks and the square brackets from the writers_id values in one transformation.

Solution

Open a custom transform window on the writers_id column and type in the following transformation expression:

value.replace("[","").replace("]","").replace("'","")

docs.title: Facets in OpenRefine
docs.text:
Facets are a useful (and powerful!) tool within OpenRefine for getting a big picture understanding of your data. Facetting groups all like values in a column together, and allows you to filter and edit those values en masse. Facets can also help you visualize your data.

OpenRefine includes several options for facets, specifically:

  • Text facets
  • Numerical facets
  • Timeline/date facets
  • Scatterplot facets
  • Custom

Text and timeline facets work much the same way: unique values are grouped together, and then listed along with the number of times that they appear in the column.

Numeric and scatterplot facets, on the other hand, display graphs instead of lists. Scatterplots, moreover, allow you to visualise the values of a pair of numeric columns, and to filter data by two-value combinations.

You can access the facetting options by clicking on the down arrow beside a variable title and then hovering over the Facet heading.

docs.title: Text facets
docs.text:
First, let's try a text facet on the movie genre variable. A text facet groups all the identical text values in a column and creates a list in a box in the left margin with the unique text values and the number of times each value appears in the faceted column.

Click the down arrow button beside the primary_genre title and hover over Facet, then click on Text Facet.

A text facet should appear as a box, labelled with the variable being facetted, on the left hand side of your window. Your primary_genre facet should have 28 choices. These can be sorted either alphabetically by name, or by count in descending order. Scroll through the list of primary genres - do you notice any errors or issues?

You should see a number of mistyped or incorrectly labelled genre titles. Let's fix one of these.

Hover over the Documntary line and click on edit when the option appears. This will open a small text window that we can use to correct the mispelling. Correct the genre title and click Apply. Notice that the film that was incorrectly labelled has now been absorbed into the correctly spelled Documentary genre.

Leave the other errors, we'll use other OpenRefine techniques to correct them.

docs.title: Facets and working with numbers
docs.text:
Let's try creating a numeric facet to get a sense of the range of average ratings of the movies in our dataset. Start by pressing the down arrow button beside ave_rating and the hover other Facet. Select Numeric facet from the option. What happened?

If something went wrong...

A facet labelled ave_rating should have appeared in the left pane in your window; however, it will not have a graph in it. Instead, it will have a message saying 'No numeric value present.' This is happening because our rating data is not correctly identified as numeric data.

When a table is imported into OpenRefine, all columns are automatically considered to be text. To fix this, we can use transformations (we'll talk more about these in a little bit).

We can transform text values into numbers by...

  1. Navigating to the dropdown menu for the column;
  2. Navigating to Edit cells;
  3. Navigating to Common transforms; and
  4. Selecting to number.

Now, transform ave_rating from text to numeric data. Once that data has been formatted to numbers, you should see the values turn green and change from left-justified to right-justified. You should also see the numeric facet for movie rating automatically update now that there is numeric data in that column.

Transform the other columns that are incorrectly formatted as text (run_time, num_votes, year).

Note

You can format the year variable as a number or a date, depending on what you want to use it for. You should transform it into date data if you want to use a timeline facet, for example. If you want to use it in a scatterplot facet, for example to investigate the relationship between movie release year and runtime, then you would want to transform it into numeric data.

Now that we have multiple numeric columns, we can use a scatterplot facet. Let's use one to look at the relationship between movie rating and movie length.

To do this, navigate to the run_time column, and click on the down arrow to access the drop down menu. From there, select Facet and then Scatterplot facet.... This will open a pop up window with a number of scatterplot option. When you hover over each, you should see a description of the variables appear. Which one should we select?

Solution

You want to select the graph that shows run_time(x) vs ave_rating (y).

What does the scatterplot tell us about the relationship between movie run time and movie rating?

docs.title: Customized facets
docs.text:
Beyond the four primary facet options (text, numeric, timeline, and scatterplot) OpenRefine also includes a number of customized facets, and allows you to write your own custom text and numeric facets.

One such useful customized facet is the facet by error. This will group your data by whether or not there are errors. Let's try making a facet by error for runtime.

On my end, a facet appears in the left side pane, but with only one item ("false") and a count of 4884. This means that there are no errors in any of the 4884 rows in my dataset.

You can close a facet by clicking the x in the top right corner of the facet.

Faceting is just one way to identify and correct errors. OpenRefine also allows us to use transformations and clustering, sometimes in conjunction with facets, to do that.

docs.title: Filtering and Sorting in OpenRefine
docs.text: OpenRefine includes a set of functions that let you sort, filter, and include or exclude data. These tools allow you to focus in on a subset of your data and can be combined with other methods.

docs.title: Filtering
docs.text:
OpenRefine includes a built-in text filter, which you can find in the same dropdown menu as the facets we've been using.

Try filtering the primary_genre column. Select the Text filter option. You should see a filter box appear in the left hand marigin of your window. Start by typing "fa". What happens?

The text filter works in real time as you type. Once you've typed "fa" you should see your data restricted to only the family and fantasy genres. You can further narrow it down by typing more.

Continue typing ntasy (so that you now have "fantasy"). You should now only have 32 entries on your browser window. You have succesfully filtered your data by fantasy genre!

Filters can be combined with facets. For example, let's take a look at the range of release dates for the fantasy movies in our dataset. Without removing the filter, create a timeline facet on the year variable.

Note

Navigate to the dropdown menu for the year column, then select Facet and Timeline facet.

What does this tell us about the date range for the fantasy movies in our dataset?

Now, remove the filter before moving on to the next operations.

How is filtering different from faceting?

These two operations look very similar, but have slightly different functions. Simply put, faceting will give you an overview of all the data selected, while filtering will select out a subset of the data to work on.

docs.title: Including and excluding
docs.text:
Including and excluding variable values is another fast way to subset your data. You can do this by hovering your cursor over an entry in a facet. When you do, options to edit and include or exclude will appear.

Let's create a facet for primary_genre again. Hover over one of the entries in that facet and click on include when it appears.

The include button appears inside the facet

You should see that your data is now limited to just that one genre. Include a second genre of your choice - what happens now?

Solution

When you include a second genre, your data will be filtered down to those two genres. The first will not be unselected.

There are three options to clearing the filter put on by including genres. First, you can close the facet.

Next, you can click on exclude beside the entry in the text facet. Try doing this to one of the entries you included earlier.

Alternatively, you can click on the reset button in the top right hand corner of the facet box. Hit that button now, and it will reset any and all inclusions or exclusions you've made.

docs.title: Sorting
docs.text:
Like filtering, sorting data is done through the column's dropdown menu (found by clicking the down arrow beside the title).

When you click on Sort... a pop up window will appear. In that window, you will get the choice to sory by text, numbers, dates, or booleans (true or false). You will also be able to choose where the blanks and errors should go in the sorted results.

Let's try sorting by text and by numbers.

First, sort primary_genre by text. When you select text in the sorting pop up window, you will have the option of whether to sort from a to z, or z to a. Leave this at the default of a to z. Also leave the order of values, errors and blanks at the default.

Second, sort run_time by number. Sort it from largest first. You'll also see an option to sort by this column alone. Leave it blank in this case, in order to sort the data by both run_time and primary_genre. You should now see the longest Action movie at the top of your table (The Tiger and the Female, at 180 minutes).

When you return to a column that you have already sorted, your options under Sort... will be slightly different. Now, you will see an option to Sort... (which will allow you to change your sorting options), Reverse (which will reverse the direction of the preexisting sort) , and Remove sort (this one is pretty self-explanatory).

Let's say we want to find out what the shortest movie in the dataset it, irrespective of genre. To do this, we'll need to remove the sort on primary genre, and reverse the sort on movie runtime. Give it a try! What is the shortest movie in the dataset?

Solution

First, navigate to primary_genre, open the dropdown menu, hover over Sort... and select Remove sort.

Now, navigate to the dropdown menu for run_time, hover over Sort... and select Reverse.

You should now get the movie "Szpieg" at the top of the table. This is the shortest movie in the dataset, at only 25 minutes long.

docs.title: Correcting mistakes
docs.text:
It's not uncommon to make a mistake, or to change your mind about something, when cleaning data. With this is mind, OpenRefine provides a very easy way to undo and redo any and all changes you've made.

In the left hand pane, you should see a tab labelled Undo/Redo. Click on it.

Every operation you've run so far will be listed in this tab. To undo changes, all you have to do is click on a previous step. To redo that change, just click on it.

Let's practice undoing a change by trying out another one of OpenRefine's column editing tools. Navitage to the genres variable and hover over Edit column. Select Split into several columns.... This will open a pop up window where you can specify how to split the column values up (by a separator or by number of characters), limit how many columns to create, and determine whether to delete the original column. Leave these at their defaults and click ok.

You should now have three columns titled genres 1, genres 2, and genres 3. For some of the rows, genres 2 and genres 3 will be blank (in these cases, the movie only has one or two genres).

Now, let's undo this change and return to our dataset with just the one genres column. Navigate to the Undo/Redo tab and select the action one above the split column action we just undertook. Your dataset should automatically revert.

docs.title: Land acknowledgement
docs.text:
Before we start the lesson, let's take a moment to think about the land on which we are learning and teaching.

I'm teaching this lesson from Edmonton, Alberta. The city of Edmonton is located on Treaty Six Territory.

This territory has been a home, a trading post, a travelling route, and more for generations of Indigenous Peoples. In particular, the nêhiyaw (Nay-hee-yow) / Cree, Dene (Deh-neyh), Anishinaabe (Ah-nish-in-ah-bay) / Saulteaux (So-toe), Nakota Isga (Na-koh-tah ee-ska) / Nakota Sioux (Na-koh-tah sue), and Niitsitapi (Nit-si-tahp-ee) / Blackfoot peoples have lived, learned, and work in this place for centuries. This land is also a homeland for the Métis, and the home of one of the largest communities of Inuit south of the 60th parallel.

In this map from native-land.ca you can see a pin representing Edmonton.

Edmonton is located within Treaty 6 Territory

Land acknowledgements are just one small piece of the work of reconciliation and must be undertaken in conjunction with other works. Acknowledging the land provides a foundation for recognizing Indigenous sovereignty and self-determination, for respecting Indigenous culture and language, and for committing to reconciliation and allyship.

docs.title: Working with Numbers in OpenRefine
docs.text:
While OpenRefine is a really powerful for cleaning text data - through facets, transformations, and clusters - it can also be used effectively to deal with numbers.

When a table is imported into OpenRefine, all columns are automatically considered to be text. To fix this, we can use transformations (as we did before).

As a reminder, we can transform text values into numbers by...

  1. Navigating to the dropdown menu for the column;
  2. Navigating to Edit cells;
  3. Navigating to Common transforms; and
  4. Selecting to number.

Transform the remainder of the number columns that are formatted as text (run_time, ave_rating, num_votes). Once they are formatted to numbers, you should see the values turn green and change from left-justified to right-justified.

Practice

Now that we have multiple numeric columns, we can use a scatterplot facet. Let's use one to look at the relationship between movie rating and movie length.

To do this, navigate to the run_time column, and click on the down arrow to access the drop down menu. From there, select Facet and then Scatterplot facet.... This will open a pop up window with a number of scatterplot option. When you hover over each, you should see a description of the variables appear. Which one should we select?

Solution

You want to select the graph that shows run_time(x) vs ave_rating (y).

What does the scatterplot tell us about the relationship between movie run time and movie rating?

Scatterplot of run time and average rating

docs.title: Saving your Work in OpenRefine
docs.text: Now that we've done all this work cleaning our data, we need to save it. As we saw when we learned about the Undo/Redo tab, OpenRefine keeps a log of every change we make to the dataset. This log is saved as a JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) file, and can be exported and applied to other files/projects.

docs.title: Exporting and saving your script
docs.text:
To export your script, you need to navigate to the Undo/Redo section of the tab in the left hand margin. Once there, click on Extract.... That will prompt a pop up window with the script of all changes made to the data. From there, click Export, and your script should automatically download as a JSON.

Note

If you were starting a new project, and wanted to use this same script (or any other that you had exported and saved), you would simply click on Apply... instead of Extract.... You would then get a pop up window with the option to either copy and paste a script or upload a script file.

docs.title: Exporting and saving your data
docs.text:
OpenRefine allows you to save your data as a new file (leaving your original data untouched) by exporting. To do so, you will need to navigate to the Export button in the top right hand corner of your browser window.

From there, you will be able to select the format in which you would like your data to be exported. There are several format options to choose from, but I would genreally recommend choosing CSV (comma-separated values).

Depending on your browser settings, your new file should automatically download. OpenRefine will name it after your project.

You also have the option to save your project. To do this, select OpenRefine project archive to file from the dropdown menu under Export. When you choose this option, OpenRefine will create one compressed file with all your data as well as all the information about the changes and transformations you did to the data. You can use this file as a project backup, or use it to share work with a collaborator, or even just use it to work on the same project on a different computer.

You can import this project back into OpenRefine by clicking on Open... in the upper right hand corner, then clicking Import Project from the dropdown menu, and finally selecting the compressed (tar.gz) file.

docs.title: Getting Started in OpenRefine
docs.text:
What is OpenRefine? OpenRefine is a free, open-source tool for cleaning and working with messy data.

OpenRefine is user-friendly and powerful. It is a great tool for that first step of research analysis - data cleaning. Here are a few reasons to use it:

  • OpenRefine automatically logs all actions;
  • OpenRefine includes easy undo and redo tools;
  • OpenRefine never modifies your original data, but rather saves your work to a new file;
  • OpenRefine works with small and large(ish) datasets of up to 100,000 rows.

OpenRefine is also a great tool for working with data that requires privacy considerations. OpenRefine works by running a small server on your computer, meaning that all data is kept on your personal computer. It does not require an internet connection, even though it does open a browser window to allow easy interaction with the software. This means that you can use it locally and offline to clean data that you want to keep secure.

Today, we're going to use OpenRefine to both clean the messy_movies.csv dataset and to answer some basic questions about the data.

docs.title: Launching OpenRefine
docs.text:
How you launch OpenRefine depends on what operating system you use. OpenRefine's documentation includes detailed instructions for how to launch the program, but here are the basics for Mac and Windows systems:

Windows: Once you've downloaded OpenRefine, navigate to the zipped file and extract it. Once it is unzipped, you can navigate into that directory and launch OpenRefine by opening openrefine.exe. This will launch a command prompt window, but just ignore that and wait for the browser to launch.

MacOS: Once you've downloaded OpenRefine, open the DMG file that was downloaded. You'll be prompted to add OpenRefine to your Applications folder. Do that, and then navigate to it and launch it. It will launch as a browser window.

In both cases, if OpenRefine does not automatically open in your browser, you can launch it by navigating to http://127.0.0.1:3333/ or http://localhost:3333.

docs.title: Creating a project
docs.text:
Once OpenRefine is launched, you will see an options to create, open, or import projects. Under these options, you'll also see tabs for language settings and extensions. For this lesson, we will be creating a new project using our "messy_movies" data. Our data is in a csv (comma separated values) format, but OpenRefine will also accept data in tsv (tab separated values), xls, xlsx, JSON, and XML formats.

Click on Create Project and then on This Computer. From there, click on Choose Files and navigate to the messy_movies.csv file you downloaded earlier, and finally click Next >> to upload the data into OpenRefine.

After uploading, OpenRefine will show you a preview of the data, giving you a chance to correct any issues in the upload before creating your project. You'll notice that OpenRefine will automatically parse the data as a file type (based on the file extension), but you can change how it parses the data if need be.

This is a great opportunity to double check that the file type was correctly identified, that your data was correctly parsed, and that all your variables are correctly titled.

Our dataset includes almost 5000 movies (4884 to be precise) and 12 variables:

  1. movie_id
  2. movie_title
  3. year
  4. runtime
  5. genres
  6. primary_genre
  7. ave_rating
  8. num_votes
  9. director_id
  10. director_name
  11. writers_id
  12. writers_name

If everything looks right to you, you can click the Create project >> buton in the upper right corner. You now have a OpenRefine project!

Once you've created your project, it will automatically open as a interactive table. Each of your variables will make up a column, with every observation getting a row. Beside each column title (variable name) you'll see a down arrow button. Clicking this button will reveal a drop down menu with a number of tools for cleaning and inspecting your data. You can also choose how many rows are shown, and navigate between pages of rows.

On the left hand side of the window, you'll see a box with two tabs: Facet/Filter and Undo/Redo. We'll explore these tabs shortly.

On the far right hand side, at the top of your window, you'll see a button labelled Help; you can click this to open OpenRefine's help documentation in a new tab.

Note.

You can work on multiple OpenRefine projects at the same time. To open a second (or a third or a fourth) project, navigate to the Open... button in the top right hand corner. This will open the landing page again, where you can create a new project, open a project that already exists on your device, or import a project.

docs.title: Using Transformations in OpenRefine
docs.text:
Transforming data can also be a quick way to correct improperly formatted data all at once. OpenRefine includes a set of common transformations that you can use, and also allows for custom transformations. The common transformations include trimming leading and trailing whitespace, changing the case of text, and even changing the data type.

The dropdown menu includes several transformation options

Practice

Let's say that we're interested in the distribution of movie releases over years. Recall that numeric facets will produce graphs - specifically, histograms. Hover over the arrow next to the year title, navigate to Facet and then to Numeric facet. What happens?

Solution

You will not be able to use a numeric facet on the year column. While the facet command will produce a facet box in the left hand margin, it will be empty. This is because the values in year are not formatted as numbers.

To fix this problem, you will need to transform the year values into numbers. To do this, follow the procedure: Facet to Common transforms to To number. When you've transformed the values into numbers, the numeric facet you made earlier should auto-populate. You'll also notice that the values in the year column are now green.

docs.title: Trimming leading and trailing whitespace
docs.text:
The transformations function can also be used to trim leading and trailing whitespaces. This is another one of the easy common transformations OpenRefine includes. Try it out now on the movie_title column. You should get a pop-up message confirming that you've changed 66 rows.

Trimming whitespace is a common transformation

docs.title: Other transformations
docs.text:
We can also use transformations to convert and clean data easily. For example, we can use transformations to turn our sets of writers’ IDs and names into clear lists of individual items. To do so, we will first need to remove the square brackets and quotation marks.

This task will require using a custom transformation. Start by clicking the down arrow beside the writer_names variable title. Choose Edit cells and then Transform. This will open a pop up window for custom transformation.

You can also write your own custom transformations

This window contains a text box, where you can type a General Refine Expression Language (GREL) and use it to transform your data.

Our first step will be to remove all the square brackets. For this, type value.replace("[","") and click ok. This GREL expression is telling OpenRefine to take every "[" and replace it with "" (nothing).

Practice

Use this same technique to remove the other square brackets (]) and the quotation marks (').

Solution

You should use the following GREL expressions:

  • value.replace("]","")
  • value.replace("'","")

After completing these two transformation, each row of writers' names should be a clean list, without any square brackets or quotation marks.

docs.title: Using Undo and Redo in OpenRefine
docs.text:
It's not uncommon to make a mistake, or to change your mind about something, when cleaning data. With this is mind, OpenRefine provides a very easy way to undo and redo any and all changes you've made.

In the left hand margin, you should see a tab labelled Undo/Redo. Click on it.

The undo/redo tab is in the left hand margin

Every operation you've run so far will be listed in this tab. To undo changes, all you have to do is click on a previous step. To redo that change, just click on it.

Practice

Try undoing all the transformations you did to the writers_name variable. Select a step before those changes and observe what happens to the variable values.

Now, re-select the most recent change. Your data should go back to how it was.
